title: PÉROLA DE MATOS v. PORTUGAL
summary: In the case of Pérola de Matos v. Portugal, the applicant, Mr. Rui André Pérola de Matos, a Portuguese national who identified as being of Roma origin, brought a complaint against Portugal. Central to his case was the harm he alleged from the use of a social report in his criminal trial, which he claimed contained discriminatory assertions about his Roma background, raising concerns about bias and the fairness of the proceedings. The events began in February 2017, when Mr. Pérola de Matos was convicted by the Leiria Criminal Court of aggravated forgery and attempted aggravated fraud, with his conviction later upheld by the Coimbra Court of Appeal in June 2018. He pursued multiple appeals, including to the Supreme Court and the Constitutional Court, arguing that the evidence used against him was tainted by discrimination and that he was denied a fair hearing. The European Court of Human Rights examined his complaints under Articles 6 (right to a fair trial), 13 (right to an effective remedy), and 14 (prohibition of discrimination), but ultimately declared the application inadmissible. The Court found that Mr. Pérola de Matos had not complied with procedural requirements, notably the six-month time limit for lodging complaints, and that his access to the Constitutional Court had not been unreasonably restricted. Although no violation was found, the case highlights the procedural hurdles Roma and Traveller applicants may face when seeking redress for discrimination in European courts, reflecting ongoing challenges in ensuring effective access to justice for these communities.
